entities.summary: Philon, Athenian architect of the 4th century BC, is known as the planner of two important works: the portico of twelve Doric columns to the great Hall of the Mysteries at Eleusis and, under the administration of Lycurgus, an arsenal in Piraeus, Athens' port city. Of the last we have exact knowledge from an inscription. E. A. Gardner observes that it "is perhaps known to us more in detail than any other lost monument of antiquity." It was to hold the rigging of the galleys; and was so contrived that all its contents were visible from a central hall, and so liable to the inspection of the Athenian democracy.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Philon's design of the Piraeus arsenal showcased innovative use of space and allowed for efficient inspection by the Athenian democracy, reflecting the city-state's emphasis on civic engagement and governance.
